paragraphs: R. Yehudah ben Bava. In the Mishnah: Eruvin 2:4, Eruvin 2:5; Yevamot 16:3, Yevamot 16:5, Yevamot 16:7; Eduyot 6:1, Eduyot 8:2. But for him, monetary penalties and ordination would have ceased. He ordained five elders: R. Meir, R. Elazar ben Shamua—Sanhedrin 14a has ben Shimon, a scribal error—R. Yehudah, R. Shimon, and R. Yosi. Some add R. Nechemyah and R. Yehudah bar Ilai; the latter is duplicated, since the unqualified R. Yehudah is bar Ilai. He was killed with three hundred arrows between Usha and Shefaram and is buried there: Gelilot Eretz Yisrael. See R. Yosi ben Kisma. See Sanhedrin, chapter 1, 13b, and Avodah Zarah 8b at length. That he never sinned: Bava Kamma, Merubbah, 80a, beginning, the story of a pious man; Temurah 15b, near the end; Jerusalem Sotah, Eglah Arufah, halakhah 10. All his deeds were for Heaven's sake, except that he raised a small animal for his health; see there at length. It explicitly identifies this man as R. Yehudah ben Bava; see R. Yehudah bar Ilai above. He is one of the ten martyrs, remembered for good: Avodah Zarah and Sanhedrin there. Yuchasin, under R. Yehudah ben Abba, writes: he lived seventy years; from age eight he slept only a horse's sleep; never called something impure pure; and fasted fifty-six years. On the day he was killed, an elder, R. Reuven Itztrobuli, wished to be killed in his place. He was fasting and pure. “To Zebulun he said: he shall dwell at the seashore” alludes to R. Yehudah ben Bava's death, sitting between two mountains and two Sabbath boundaries and being killed: Recanati, Vayechi. Gilgulei Neshamot says Yonatan ben Gershom is the pious man in Yalkut Ruth, on “Is this Naomi?” A pious man undertook not to accept anything from anyone, etc., until he had to sit on a refuse heap. Elijah appeared as an Arab and asked, “Would you like me to lend you two silver coins, with which to trade and live?” He agreed. Elijah gave him the coins. He bought goods and profited. Before a year passed he became wealthy and forgot his piety and prayer. The Holy One, blessed be He, told Elijah, “I had one pious man in My world, and you obstructed him from Me.” He went and found him engaged in a great enterprise. He said, “I gave you two selaim; return them.” He returned them, lost his property, and again sat weeping on the refuse heap. Elijah returned, etc., and said, “If you swear that, should I return those two selaim, you will preserve your times of piety and practice of prayer ...” He agreed, took the two silver coins, and grew wealthy, etc. He had been Shevuel ben Gershom ben Manasseh, namely Yonatan, who became an idolatrous priest to avoid depending on others. David saw that money was dear to him and appointed him over the treasuries. He was called Shevuel because he returned to God with all his heart: see Bava Batra 110a. When David died, Solomon replaced and removed him, and he returned to corruption, etc. He repented, and the holy spirit rested on him, as in “The word of the Lord came to the prophet who brought him back.” He was therefore reincarnated as this poor pious man, refusing to accept from anyone, just as he had hired himself to idolatry to avoid dependence on others. You already know the sages' statement that an unqualified “pious man” in a story is R. Yehudah ben Bava or R. Yehudah bar Ilai; see there. There, he first went astray when poor; when wealthy, he was upright and pious, so David appointed him over the treasuries. When Solomon removed him, he returned to his waywardness. Here, when poor he was pious and upright, recognizing his own station and accepting sufferings lovingly. Elijah wished to test whether he would remain as pious while wealthy. He did not withstand the test until returning to poverty; therefore Elijah eventually made him wealthy, and he remained pious. This was his complete repair. End of quotation. The aforementioned R. Yehudah the priest was his colleague. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, his colleague—this requires investigation. And Shimon HaTimni.
